query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A phase‐selective recrystallization treatment applied to the eutectic high-entropy alloy will mitigate the dislocation pile-ups at the internal lamellar boundaries, thereby reducing local stress concentrations and microcracking; this will lead to enhanced room‐temperature ductility while retaining or even increasing the strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies composed of (typically) a ductile FCC phase and a hard B2/BCC phase, where dislocation pile-ups at semi‐coherent internal boundaries cause stress concentration and brittle failure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low‐temperature annealing protocol (phase‐selective recrystallization) to selectively recrystallize the ductile FCC phase along the lamellar interfaces while preserving the hard phase and its strong semi‐coherent boundaries.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile testing representative of typical service conditions; annealing parameters must be optimized to affect only the ductile phase without coarsening the hard phase (e.g., specific temperature and time windows determined via preliminary studies).
generation.structural_mediator: The intervention produces recrystallized FCC regions with reduced and more uniformly distributed dislocation density; this minimizes the severity of dislocation pile-ups at the internal (lamellar) phase boundaries without degrading the potent strengthening effect of the semi-coherent boundaries from the hard phase.
generation.mechanism: Selective annealing relieves localized internal stresses by reducing the dislocation density within the FCC phase, thereby lessening local stress concentrations and microcrack nucleation at phase boundaries. At the same time, the preserved strong interfaces maintain or promote work hardening, ensuring that the overall strength is retained or improved.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the phase-selectively recrystallized material should display significantly higher uniform elongation (potentially increasing ductility from modest values to around 35% uniform elongation) while exhibiting yield and ultimate tensile strengths at or exceeding levels near 2 GPa.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA shows limited room-temperature ductility and brittleness due to pronounced dislocation pile-ups at the dual-phase lamellar boundaries, leading to premature microcracking.
generation.boundary: The success of the treatment depends critically on precise control of the annealing parameters. Over-annealing or non-selective recrystallization could degrade the microstructure (e.g., loss of lamellar alignment or coarsening of phases) and negate the strength–ductility benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements (in percentage elongation and strength values) are sensitive to the specific processing window and alloy composition; further optimization is needed to define the optimal treatment conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic HEA. Subject one set to the controlled phase-selective annealing treatment aimed at recrystallizing the FCC phase while maintaining the hard lamellar structure, and leave the other set untreated. Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets and conduct in situ TEM analyses to monitor dislocation behavior near the internal boundaries.
measurements: Dislocation density and pile-up characteristics near phase boundaries (via TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in ductility (e.g., uniform elongation enhancement) without a loss of strength compared to the untreated samples, or if TEM reveals no substantial reduction in or redistribution of dislocation pile-ups at the phase boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Dislocation substructures, such as dense dislocation walls (Fig. 3d) and dislocation networks (Fig. S5), were developed at the final stage of uniform plastic deformation and dragged on crack propagation. Although BCC phases were strengthening components in the eutectic dual-phase HEA due to their intrinsically large lattice resistance, which made them hard to deform plastically, the existence of semi-coherent phase boundaries played an essential part in balancing strength-ductility. Considering the brittleness of ordered BCC phases, the unexpected strong phase boundaries can prevent massive dislocations from penetrating, thus not only reducing dislocation pile-ups in BCC phases, which may facilitate the nucleation of cracks, but also promoting work hardening process in FCC phases by achieving dense dislocation storage.

Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
